National Weather Service Burlington VT
638 AM EST Mon Nov 9 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 124 AM EST Monday...

No significant changes were made with this forecast update.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 124 AM EST Monday...

1. Upper low pressure will keep the weather unsettled through 
the middle of the week. 

2. Monitoring the potential for wintry weather over the 
weekend, and plenty of model spread/uncertainty remains.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 124 AM EST Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: More of the same dreary weather expected for the first 
half of the week. We remain on the periphery of upper low pressure 
centered near the Gaspe Peninsula early this morning, with patchy 
light rain and drizzle occurring across much of the region. This 
activity is associated with a shortwave trough rounding the base of 
the trough, and we'll see a series of these over the next 48-72 
hours. As such, periods of showers will continue to plague the 
region, particularly today and then again Tuesday into Tuesday 
night. As has been the case, most of the precipitation will fall as 
rain, with areas AOA 2500 ft mixing with and/or changing to snow 
overnight and into the early morning hours. A reinforcing shot of 
cold air Tuesday night will bring snow levels as low as 1500 ft or 
so, mainly along the international border and the northern 
Adirondacks/Greens, and this is the best chance for seeing any 
accumulating snow below 2000 ft, though even then, it'll be pretty 
minimal. The cold pool aloft and some meager instability could allow 
for more robust showers to produce some graupel both this afternoon 
and Tuesday afternoon, along with brief moderately heavy rainfall. 
Daytime temperatures will be similar both days, mainly in the mid 
40s to low 50s, with the southern St Lawrence/Champlain Valleys 
approaching the mid 50s Tuesday afternoon under increasing W/SW 
flow. These winds will be on the breezy side Tuesday and Tuesday 
evening, particularly at summit level and on the eastern slopes of 
the Adirondacks and central/southern Greens. Gusts to 30 mph will be 
possible in these locations, with 35 to 45+ mph atop the mountain 
summits. Wednesday is looking to be the driest day, with shower 
coverage to be confined to the Northeast Kingdom and mainly during 
the morning hours. Some sunshine might break through in the 
afternoon, but it will remain seasonably cool with highs remaining 
in the 40s to around 50F.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A fairly messy weather pattern will prevail for the 
latter half of the week. Temperatures appear likely to be about the 
same from day-to-day with upper 30s to mid 40s during the day and 
20s to lower 30s at night. A high amplitude ridge will build across 
the western US while a pair of shortwaves dig well into the 
southeastern US on Thursday. These will eventually interact with the 
persistent upper low to our north during the weekend. Depending on 
the exact track of surface low pressure, the interaction between the 
various upper vorts, and which will be most intense will affect the 
outlook for Friday into Saturday. Given the broad, disorganized 
nature of the upper level features, it seems likely that the thermal 
gradient and active subtropical jet could be the deciding factors, 
which would favor suppressed, southern solutions. However, raw 
ensemble probabilities (both statistical, AI-driven and physics-
based forecasts) suggest it is worth monitoring the potential for 
accumulating snow in our forecast area. We recently highlighted 
preparedness for winter weather across New England, and so it is 
good to be ready whether or not something takes place. Given the 
temperature forecast, this would likely be a wet snow with some rain 
potential in the valleys, and if there is much in the way of snow, 
accumulations will depend on elevation. Weather will turn cool under 
northwest flow heading into Sunday and Monday, with orographic, 
upslope snow showers possible.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Through 12Z Tuesday...A surface trough is shifting east of the
area now, but an upper low is moving overhead now. This is
resulting in showers mainly over the Adirondacks and south-
central Vermont. Ceilings range from around 1000-3500 ft agl. 
Winds have been variable, and will likely remain so through 
about 13-14z. Winds will turn northwesterly today, and some
scattered showers will likely develop during the afternoon.
Ceilings could remain fairly steady today, and there could be
some localized lower visibility in heavier rain showers or lower
ceilings, mainly at KSLK or KEFK. Surface winds will likely peak
around sunset through about 00-02z round 7-13 knots sustained
with gusts 16-20 knots possible. As winds subside after 04z,
ceilings are expected to trend lower. Any terminal at VFR will
likely trend MVFR.

Outlook...

Tuesday: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Tuesday Night: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Veterans Day: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.
Wednesday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight
chance SN.
Thursday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight chance RA.
Thursday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance RA,
Chance SN.
Friday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Chance RA, Chance
SN.

&&
